title: States, amplitudes & measurement
source: Lecture Slides - 1 to 7.pdf, PDF pages 14–20; Practice Problems Q1–5, Q10; introductory transcript used for teaching context.
objectives: Explain why phase can matter even when Z-basis probabilities do not change.
body:
From probabilities to amplitudes

A classical random bit is described by probabilities that sum to one. A pure qubit is described by two complex amplitudes: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩. Their squared magnitudes sum to one: |α|² + |β|² = 1.

Computational-basis measurement returns 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|². One measurement gives one classical outcome; it does not reveal both amplitudes.

A worked example

For |ψ⟩ = [|0⟩ + (1 + 3i)|1⟩]/√11, the squared magnitudes are 1/11 and (1² + 3²)/11 = 10/11. They add to one, so the state is normalized. This works through practice question Q1.

Keep this distinction

Amplitudes can interfere. Probabilities are real, nonnegative numbers obtained after taking squared magnitudes.

Explore a pure qubit

Up to global phase, |ψ⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + exp(iφ) sin(θ/2)|1⟩. The Bloch coordinates are (sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ, cos θ). Change φ while holding θ fixed. Predict which measurement probabilities will change.

quiz.question: With θ = π/2, changing φ from 0 to π changes which quantity?
quiz.explanation: Z-basis probabilities remain 1/2. The state changes from |+⟩ to |−⟩, so the X-basis probability of + changes from 1 to 0.

exercise: Solve Q2–5 and Q10 in your practice sheet. For Q2, use |1−i|² = 2 before normalizing.
solution: Q2: N = 1/√6 and vector (1−i, 2)ᵀ/√6. Q10: θ=π/2, φ=π gives |−⟩.
